sources.entry: Startup Lessons Learned - Five Whys - Eric Ries *(creator of the Lean Startup)*

summary.title: Five Whys
summary.one_liner: Learn how to run blameless post-mortems by asking "why" five times to find root causes, then invest proportionally in fixes, as Eric Ries describes from his time at IMVU.
takeaways: Ask 'why' repeatedly (about five times) after an incident to move past the technical symptom to the human and process root cause.
Run post-mortems with everyone involved, have one facilitator lead, and assign owners for fixes.
Share the five whys write-up company-wide in plain English so people understand the problems and the investment in prevention.
Invest in fixes roughly in proportion to the cost of the problem, with a maximum and a minimum, rather than rewriting everything.
Layered defenses (sandboxes, tests, CI gating, automated staged deploys, alerting) give the five whys process concrete questions to ask and improve over time.
summary.summary: Eric Ries argues that when something goes wrong, teams should run a post-mortem and ask "why" about five times to reach the root cause, which often turns out to be a process or people problem rather than a purely technical one. He explains how to start: pick a team and problem class, appoint a single five-whys facilitator, gather everyone involved, and send the plain-English result to the whole company. He recommends investing in fixes proportionally to the problem's cost, with a minimum and maximum. He illustrates the approach with IMVU's layered deployment defenses and closes by crediting Taiichi Ohno and the Toyota Production System.
